messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

Noam is out of town, so I will be there to provide cookies and moral support for our regular D-RUG meeting in Wickson 2124 from 1-3 PM.

Hope to see you there!

~ Kristina

Kristina Wolf
Restoration Ecology Lab
Ph.D. Candidate, Graduate Group in Ecology
Department of Plant Sciences
B.S. Animal Science, M.S. Soil Science
(530) 750-9771

"We have to remember that what we observe is not nature herself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning." ~ Werner Heisenberg

messages.subject: Next Week: Tim Bowles on the vegan package
messages.subject_clean: Next Week: Tim Bowles on the vegan package
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Next week at D-RUG, Tim Bowles will teach a short workshop on the vegan <http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/vegan/index.html> package. From Tim:
>
> Getting into the meat of vegan (yup, that was intended): Do you work with community and environment data? Or did you measure too many variables that are more or less related to each other and need to wade through them? Or have data with a lot more variables than samples (e.g. gene expression, spectroscopy)? Then vegan, a package for community analysis, might be useful for you. While vegan was designed with analysis of species/environment relationships in mind, it’s useful anytime you want to implement many standard multivariate techniques in R.
>
> I will walk through some of the basics of vegan, including: how to do ordination (PCA and NMDS); relating community data to environmental variables through constrained ordination (RDA) and vector overlaying; and permutational analysis of variance. I will also go over dissecting vegan’s ordination output to produce pretty graphs that are publication ready. vegan also has functions for analysis of biodiversity (e.g. calculation of diversity indices, species abundance models) but I will not cover them.

We’ll meet at the regular time and place (Tuesday 1:10-3, Wickson 2124*), and of course, there will be cookies. We will also screencast the talk at this link: http://goo.gl/S2iIn8, though I have yet to successfully cookie-cast.

Noam

*Wheelchair accessible via ramp at main entrance, elevators at East and West sides of building.

messages.subject: How to get median of all measurements within radius
messages.subject_clean: How to get median of all measurements within radius
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I'm comparing local medians to other models as a predictor of arsenic in groundwater. Can anyone help me with the code below? Database attached as well if needed. Thanks in advance!

#How can I get the median of all measurements within 2000 meters?
#There's probably a better way, but since I'm new to R and already had the IDW code set up,
#I've been trying to do it that way, setting the weighting power (idp) near zero so closer points are weighted the same as far ones.
#I'm guessing it says NA when maxdist=2000 because some points don't have any neighbors within 2000 meters.
#The smallest maxdist I can get it to work with is ~40,000, even if I set nmin to zero. Is there a way to tell it
#to ignore points without neighbors within 2000 meters, or does someone know a better way to do this?

library(gstat)
clean3145 = read.csv("clean3145.csv")

#Set up the k-fold validation
set.seed(88)
groups <- sample(1:5, nrow(clean3145), replace=TRUE)

#res=result=R=Pearson's correlation between predicted and actual arsenic concentration
#NEAREST=single nearest neighbor, MED=median within radius, IDW=inverse distance weighted interpolation

NEARESTres <- MEDres<- IDWres <- rep(NA, 5)

r <- list()
for (k in 1:5) {
  print(k)
  flush.console()
  train <- clean3145[groups!=k, ]
  test <- clean3145[groups==k, ]

  nearest <- gstat(formula = As1~1, locations = ~UTMNM+UTMEM, data=train, nmax=1)
  nearestpred <- predict(nearest, test)$var1.pred
  NEARESTres[k] <- cor(test$As1, nearestpred)

  med <- gstat(formula = As1~1, locations = ~UTMNM+UTMEM, data=train, nmin=0, maxdist=40000, set=list(idp = .01))
  medpred <- predict(med, test)$var1.pred
  MEDres[k] <- cor(test$As1, medpred)

  idw <- gstat(formula = As1~1, locations = ~UTMNM+UTMEM, data=train, nmax=4, set=list(idp = .56))
  idwpred <- predict(idw, test)$var1.pred
  IDWres[k] <- cor(test$As1, idwpred)

  }

#Show the mean correlation for the 5 different training-test dataset pairs in K-fold validation
mean(NEARESTres)
mean(MEDres)
mean(IDWres)

messages.subject: blocked split-plot anova
messages.subject_clean: blocked split-plot anova
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to analyse a blocked split plot design in lme4 or nlme and would like some help in making sure I am using the correct code.

The design I have is a blocked split-plot design with repeated measures so I have 2 between-plot and 2 within-plot effects.
There are 3 random blocks on the landscape with two fences in each block. Each fence is split and has either a winter warming (WW) or no winter warming (WC). On either side of the fence there are 4 sub-plots, 2 of which have a summer warming treatment (SW) and 2 of which have no summer warming (SC). Every sub-plot is monitored once a year for 5 years. The question is whether carbon flux changes significantly between treatments and through time.

It looks like this:

3 blocks replicated on the landscape, random between-subject effect
2 fences nested in each block, this is the unit of replication for my fixed between-subject effect WW described below, these are coded 1-6 so that each fence in each block has a unique ID
1 treatment applied to each fence, either WW or WC, fixed between- subject effect
1 treatment crossed with each treatment at the fence level, either SW or SC, these are applied in 2 sub-plots per fence, fixed within-subject effect
this produces WWxSW, WWxSC, WCxSW and WCxSC treatments
each sub-plot is monitored once per year for 5 years, fixed within-subject effect

I want to make sure my variables are coded correctly. Currently each fence is unique 1:6, blocks are A,B,C and sub-plots are 1:8, repeated in every block/fence combination. This makes sense to me, the fences and blocks are unique; plot 1 in every block/fence comes from the same treatment and, if treatment has an effect, they should behave similarly regardless of where they are on the landscape. I think this way block/fence will be my unit of replication for the WW effect and sub-plot my unit of replication for repeated measures in years.

Here is my code attempt:

model.nlme <- lme (carbon ~ WW*SW*year,
                      random=~1|block/fence/WW/SW/sub-plot,
                    data = flux.cum.treat.plot,method="REML")

anova(model.nlme)
            numDF denDF   F-value p-value
(Intercept)     1   188  94.03039  <.0001
WW              1     5   1.94065  0.2224
SW              1    10   0.19706  0.6666
year            1   188 190.17488  <.0001
WW:SW           1    10   0.95409  0.3517
WW:year         1   188   5.20715  0.0236
SW:year         1   188   0.07169  0.7892
WW:SW:year      1   188   1.33104  0.2501

Is this correct?
One thing that is a little puzzling to me is why year has only 1DF? Shouldn't it be 4?

However, this does not work in lmer. Why?

model <- lmer(carbon ~ WW*SW*year +     # these are my fixed effects, WW is between-subject and SW, year are within-subject
                 (1|block/fence/WW/SW/year/sub-plot),
               data = flux.cum.treat.plot)
Error in checkNlevels(reTrms$flist, n = n, control) :
  number of levels of each grouping factor must be < number of observations

I know that lme4 is the more favoured package, I started using nlme because I want to be able to define the covariance structure as autoregressive (AR1), which I do not think lme4 can do. But why does nlme accept sub-plot as a nested factor and lme4 does not?

Does the hierarchy of fixed or random effects matter, as long as the order of nesting is correct? If I have my fixed effect in the y ~ x + z part of the formula, will it always be considered fixed?

I have read some suggestions that it is good coding practice to have a different data column for the main and nested variable, even if they are identical. In my case that would be eg: WW_fixed, WW_nested. Is this purely for coding clarity?

Thanks very much for any help,
Marguerite

*********
This questions is quite similar to Emily Peffer's post from some time ago:
ANOVA with nested random and fixed effects: help!
The biggest difference is that my largest unit of observation, the block, is random, so are block/fence and sub-plot. Based on the discussion in that thread, I think my model.nlme should be right.

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: blocked split-plot ANOVA with fixed and random effects
messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: blocked split-plot ANOVA with fixed and random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marguerite,

I had a similar coding debacle about a year ago that involved multiple levels of nesting and random and fixed effects (ugh!), but I think I finally figured it out using lme.

Try this:

#your 'fence' effect is equivalent to your winter warming effect (main plot- I'm calling it WWWC), so you don't need to have both in your model
#I'm calling your summer warming trt (subplot) SCSW
#first line has all your fixed effects, second line specifies nesting structure of random effects

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW,
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW,
       data=data)

As far as data organization, I think that as long as your model is specified correctly, it doesn't matter much how you number your variables. Just have one column for each factor in your model, and make sure that R knows that everything is a factor.

Hope that helps,
Emily

messages.body_plain:
Marguerite,

If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.

Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1).

Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:

lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW,
       random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
       data=data)

Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1).

You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in.

Emily

On Monday, December 8, 2014 4:08:59 PM UTC-5, Emily Peffer wrote:
> Marguerite,
>
> If I'm understanding your design correctly, you have fences (main plots) randomized within blocks, which is the same as saying you have WW nested in blocks. Then, you assigned two subplots to each main plot, which is the same as saying you nested SW within WW (or fence). Therefore, you could either use fences or WW in your model, and you could use subplots or WW, but I don't think you want to have both in your model.
>
> Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1).
>
> Year is tricky, and where you should put it in your model probably depends on the purpose of taking measurements over time and what kind of inferences you want to make. For example, if you are really interested in the overall effect of each year, I could see putting it as your highest nesting factor (blocks nested in year, and so-on). But you said you want sub-plot to be your unit of replication for year, which means it would go at the end (i.e., year becomes a sort of 'sub-sub-plot'). So your model would look like this:
>
> lme(carbon~year*WWWC*SCSW,
>        random=~1|Block/WWWC/SCSW/year,
>        data=data)
>
> Then, I believe your DF for year should be 4 (5 years-1).
>
> You might want to consult with a statistician about what the appropriate degrees of freedom are for each factor given your design, and then make sure your model matches that. Knowing what the appropriate tests are for each factor gets tricky when you have a complicated design like this. Or perhaps someone with more experience in repeated measures designs could weigh in.

messages.body_plain:
Just to confirm- each fence has only one WW treatment, right? So each block has two different WW treatments? If so, fence is your experimental unit for WW. You are not really interested in the effect of fence, correct? The reason to include block in the model is because you randomized WW treatments within block (2 fences, one treatment per fence). Therefore, some of the error within your treatments may be attributable to areas on the landscape, and you want to reduce this source of error. But I still don't see why you would include fence. The way the model that includes fence in your last email is set up, it's saying your WW treatment is nested in fence, which is nested in block. But WW is not really nested in fence if there's only one treatment applied to the fence. If you didn't have a WW treatment, and only had a SW treatment, then your SW would be nested in fence, because there are two treatments per fence. Unless I am misunderstanding your design.

I think the error in your last model is because you include fence and sub-plot.  If you look at your "Number of groups", the numbers within each group are inflated.

I think it's okay to use anova() for the lme output. One thing to be aware of is that it uses Type I (sequential) sums of squares. There's a big debate about which type of SS is most appropriate for different designs and goals, but the conclusion I came to was that Type I was best for nested designs.

Hopefully a statistician, or someone on this listserv with more statistical prowess, can help confirm how to appropriately specify your model. Let me know what you end up with, I'm curious!

Emily

messages.subject: Re: Next Week: Tim Bowles on the vegan package
messages.subject_clean: Next Week: Tim Bowles on the vegan package
messages.body_plain:
Hi again!

Does anyone know, will the whole session today be about vegan, or will there also be time to work on our own projects?

Thanks, hope you're all enjoying the tule fog!

El jueves, 4 de diciembre de 2014 15:01:31 UTC-8, Noam Ross escribió:
>
> Hi all,
>
> Next week at D-RUG, Tim Bowles will teach a short workshop on the vegan <http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/vegan/index.html> package. From Tim:
> >
> > Getting into the meat of vegan (yup, that was intended): Do you work with community and environment data? Or did you measure too many variables that are more or less related to each other and need to wade through them? Or have data with a lot more variables than samples (e.g. gene expression, spectroscopy)? Then vegan, a package for community analysis, might be useful for you. While vegan was designed with analysis of species/environment relationships in mind, it’s useful anytime you want to implement many standard multivariate techniques in R.
> >
> > I will walk through some of the basics of vegan, including: how to do ordination (PCA and NMDS); relating community data to environmental variables through constrained ordination (RDA) and vector overlaying; and permutational analysis of variance. I will also go over dissecting vegan’s ordination output to produce pretty graphs that are publication ready. vegan also has functions for analysis of biodiversity (e.g. calculation of diversity indices, species abundance models) but I will not cover them.
>
> We’ll meet at the regular time and place (Tuesday 1:10-3, Wickson 2124*), and of course, there will be cookies. We will also screencast the talk at this link: http://goo.gl/S2iIn8, though I have yet to successfully cookie-cast.
>
> Noam
>
> *Wheelchair accessible via ramp at main entrance, elevators at East and West sides of building.
> ​
>

messages.body_plain:
Oh yeah, this helps. This is different than what I was imagining. I thought each fence was entirely one WW treatment or the other, and I didn't realize there were replications of SW within the main plot.

So from this diagram it looks to me like your blocks aren't really necessary to include. Normally a block is split into sub-units that are different (like plots that get different treatments) but in your case, each fence has the same combination of treatments.  Your fences are acting like blocks in this diagram, with each fence split into two main plots (WW and WC) and each main plot split into four subplots (SW and SC). If you include fence, that will take care of the spatial variation that would also be attributable to block, so I see no need to include both. So I'd structure the model like this:

lme(carbon~WWWC*SCSW*Year,
       random=~1|Fence/WWWC/SCSW/subplot/Year,
       data=data)

Whether you use * or + in the first line has to do with what interactions you're interested in, so that might need to be changed. Because your individual yearly measurements are made on subplots, I do think you need to include subplot, but I'm not 100% sure.

Emily

Normally a block is split into sub-units that are different (like plots that get different treatments) but in your case, each fence has the same combination of treatments.  Your fences are acting like blocks in this diagram, with each fence split into two main plots (WW and WC) and each main plot split into four subplots (SW and SC). >        random=~1|Fence/WWWC/SCSW/subplot/Year,
>        data=data)

Hi Emily,

I should have added that diagram to start with. Pictures are useful. I had to make that for myself when I started working on this project because I kept (and apparently still am) getting hopelessly confused.

As far as I understand these things, I think that your suggested model is correct, but I am still not sure about including subplot in the nesting structure. It puts all my units of replication into the grouping factors and I'm not entirely sure how the model deals with that. I think that nlme doesn't like it but just ignores it, lme4 just won't run.

Once I have triangulated various pieces of information I will post the solution I came up with. I'm also curious what Jaime will come back with.

Thanks so much for your input, it has been really helpful!
Marguerite

Normally a block is split into sub-units that are different (like plots that get different treatments) but in your case, each fence has the same combination of treatments.  Your fences are acting like blocks in this diagram, with each fence split into two main plots (WW and WC) and each main plot split into four subplots (SW and SC). >        random=~1|Fence/WWWC/SCSW/subplot/Year,
>        data=data)

messages.body_plain:
Hello dear Davis R users,

I am unfortunately rather stumped on what seems to be a simple problem.

I want to compare the attached data ("SampleData") by each column of
species information (Sp1,2 & 3), to a column of mean information -
"CompValue" by "Site", to generate a dataframe which says whether the
species has "Higher" or "Lower" values than the means.

I thought I could do this by using apply by columns and an ifelse
statement, but I seem to be setting that up wrong somehow, and perhaps I
need another argument in the apply function to indicate that the value
for each column needs to be compared to the corresponding site
comparison value (across rows). I have tried ddply and by and it seems
that I am missing something about how to logically set this up.

Any help much appreciated. The attached files are Sample Data and Sample
Result to get an idea of what I have and where I want to go.

Thanks!,
Stella

--
Stella Copeland
Post-doctoral Researcher
Harrison Lab, Plant Ecology
UC Davis

messages.body_plain:
Here’s a dplyr implementation:
library(dplyr)

SampleData = structure(list(Site = 1:6, Sp1 = c(25L, 30L, NA, 62L, 10L, 5L
), Sp2 = c(15, 3, 4, 2, 1, 0.1), Sp3 = c(3L, 3L, 3L, NA, 4L,
90L), CompValue = c(15L, 10L, 2L, 5L, 6L, 4L)), .Names = c("Site",
"Sp1", "Sp2", "Sp3", "CompValue"), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA,
-6L))

SampleResult = SampleData %>%
    mutate_each(funs(ifelse( . > CompValue, "High", "Low")), starts_with("Sp")) %>%
        select(-CompValue)

SampleResult
  Site  Sp1  Sp2  Sp3 CompValue
1    1 High  Low  Low        15
2    2 High  Low  Low        10
3    3 <NA> High High         2
4    4 High  Low <NA>         5
5    5 High  Low  Low         6
6    6 High  Low High         4

mutate_each takes SampleData and modifies any column selected with the last argument (starts_with("Sp")) using the function defined inside funs, where . stands for the input. The last line drops CompValue.
​

Noam

d = read.csv("Oceanographic data BML buoy 2014.csv")

messages.body_plain:
The code seems to do what you want it to - make the graph with an axis that shows dates at the bottom in DD/MM format.  I'm not sure what your question is.  There is some redundancy in the code but it's fine.  But here's an explanation of what's going on:

d = read.csv("Oceanographic data BML buoy 2014.csv")
newdata = d[6141:11574, ] #  subsets data for the dates I'm interested in

times = strptime(newdata$INSTRUMENT_DATETIME, format="%m/%d/%y  %H:%M") #converts the dates (character format) to POSIXlt format.  POSIXlt represents times as lists of sec/min/hour/... etc value.  They are not the easiest format to manipulate
times = as.POSIXct(times) # This converts from POSIXlt to POSIXct, in which the information is stored as seconds from the start of 1970

plot(times,newdata$CHLOROPHYLL,
     type="l", ylab="Chlorophyll a (μg/L)", xlab="", xaxt="n")

times2=format(times, "%m/%d") #This creates character strings in MM/DD format from the POSIXct info.  Other info (time, year, timezone, etc.), is lost.
times2<-as.POSIXct(times2, format="%m/%d") #This converts back to POSIXct. Since it only has date and month, it assumes current year, local timezone, and midnight time. By default, when displaying POSIXct values with times of exactly midnight, the time is not shown, only dates.
S=seq(as.POSIXct(times2[1]),as.POSIXct(times2[length(times2)]), by="3 days") #This, which is actually calling the seq.POSIXct method, makes a sequence of values from the beginning to the end of "times2", with 3-day intervals between them.  The as.POSIXct calls inside are redundant.
axis.POSIXct(1,times2,at=S,label=S,format="%m/%d", las=2) #This creates an axis on the bottom (side 1), using the values in S and displaying the labels in S.  The only difference between it and a normal "axis" call is that it takes the "format" argument, which here says to display the labels in MM/DD format.  The "las" argument determines the alignment of text.

More on Dates/Times in Bonnie's excellent notes from her presentation at D-RUG last Feb: http://www.noamross.net/blog/2014/2/10/using-times-and-dates-in-r---presentation-code.html

Noam

messages.body_plain:
Ah, the year was getting cut off because of my window size.

You’re getting years because of the labels argument in
axis.POSIXct(1,times2,at=S,label=S,format="%m/%d", las=2)

R expects the label argument to be a character vector of labels to put on the axis. It gets S, a POSIXct vector, so it converts it to characters with default methods, which displays the date. The label argument overrides automatic labeling, which would take the values in the at argument and convert them using the format argument. Remove label=S, and you get MM/DD labels.
​

messages.subject: Subsetting a data frame using a critiera: exclude if the sum of row or column equals zero; if the rowname has certain characters present
messages.subject_clean: Subsetting a data frame using a critiera: exclude if the sum of row or column equals zero; if the rowname has certain characters present
messages.body_plain:
Hi gang,

New to the R User's Group and have heard only good things about the community.

So here is my issue. I would like to subset rows and columns that meet a certain condition into a new data frame. If the sum of the row or column = 0, then it is not included in the new data frame. Additionally, I would like to subset data based on a criteria looking at the rownames (or I guess it could be just a site name in a column). This seems like a fairly straight forward problem but I am pretty new to R... Any help would be greatly appreciated. I hope the code below makes it clear what I am asking.

My data looks something like the data frame produced below.

col1 <- c(1,0,0,2,5,1,0)
col2 <- c(0,0,1,1,1,0,0)
col3 <- c(0,0,0,0,0,0,0)
col4 <- c(0,0,1,1,0,1,0)
rownames(testdataframe) <- c("CA1","CA2","CA3","CA4","LN1","LN2","LN3")
testdataframe <- data.frame(col1, col2, col3, col4)

testdataframe_subset <- testdataframe[-(if sum of row = 0, exclude),-(if sum of column = 0, exclude)]

So, testdataframe_subset would look like testdataframe[c(1,3:7),c(1,2,4)]

testdataframe_subset_ca <- testdataframe_subset[(if first two letters in rowname = "CA")]

So, testdataframe_subset_ca would look like testdataframe_subset[c(1:3),]

Perhaps the solution is something like all[which(condition)] but I am not sure.

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Subsetting a data frame using a critiera: exclude if the sum of row or column equals zero; if the rowname has certain characters present
messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: Subsetting a data frame using a critiera: exclude if the sum of row or column equals zero; if the rowname has certain characters present
messages.body_plain:
Kousei,

Your instincts are very close. Here’s a command for excluding zero-sum rows or columns.
testdataframe_subset = testdataframe[!(rowSums(testdataframe) == 0), !(colSums(testdataframe) == 0)]

The colSums and rowSums do what you’d expect. Note that you don’t need which here. which translates the vectors of TRUE/FALSE results returned by the x == 0 commands to numbers, but you can subset based on TRUE/FALSE as well as numbers. Note that ! reverses the TRUE/FALSE values.

To subset by rowname:
testdataframe_subset_ca = testdataframe_subset[grepl("^CA", rownames(testdataframe_subset)),]

grepl searches for it’s first argument in all the values of the second argument and returns TRUE/FALSE values. Note that "^CA" is a regular expression meaning “starts with CA”. See ?regex for more details.

Noam
​

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: blocked split-plot ANOVA with fixed and random effects
messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: blocked split-plot ANOVA with fixed and random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marguerite,

Sorry for the delay in responding. Thanks for providing the details.

With the disclaimer that I Am Not a Statistician, without randomization of whole plot factors to whole plots (fence sides) and split-plot factors to subplots, the assumptions of a split-plot design aren't met. In your case the first randomization maybe isn't too meaningful (ie maybe the fence orientations are already random), but the second seems important and lacking in the design you're analyzing. Talking to a statistician seems like a good idea, but be prepared for a bad response given the lack of randomization!

If the assumptions WERE met, specification of a split plot follows Pinheiro/Bates Oats example (see section 1.6 of their book, or the code available here https://www.stat.wisc.edu/courses/st850-lindstro/handouts/splitplotlme.pdf) Your example would have some differences. Below is my understanding of how they would work in nlme/lmer

- In Oats each treatment of the split plot factor is only applied to one subplot, while in your case there are two, this introduces another level of nesting at the (physical) spilt plot level.  Specifying this in the Oats example would be redundant to the fixed effects on nitro (something like yield ~  Variety * ordered(nitro) + (1 | Block/Variety/nitro) which causes an error because there's one Block:Variety:nitro level for each observation!)

- Your repeated measures, which are also part of the question (is there a change over time?). Specifying RE at the subplot level will also take care of this, with no need to year in the RE term. Adding year will make the model saturated. m_simple below implements this (and is the same as Emily's suggestion but without Year as the final level of RE). Simply specifying within-subplot RE doesn't formally account for temporal autocorrelation within subplot -- to do that see ?nlme::corAR1). First just look at random slope on year (see below). I think this is the best option and if the within-subplot residuals look ok corAR1 isn't necessary.

- Fences within Blocks: this is worth trying to account for but there may not be the data to estimate it

# Questions: whether carbon flux changes significantly between treatments and through time.

# make unique variables for each nested unit
# this makes sthings clearer to you and
# if you use lme4 it will then recognize the implicit nesting
data <- within(data, {
    wholeplot <- factor(block:fence:WW)
    subplot <- factor(block:fence:WW:SW)
})

m_simple <- lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year,
       random= ~ 1 |fence/wholeplot/subplot,
       data=data)

## this (or analogous version accounting for block) makes most sense as it allows for with subplot differences in response and could be implemented in lme or lmer
## it seems necessary if data show variation in temporal trend within WWWC:SCSW combinations but the fit may be unhealthy (very high correlation between slope and intercept within subplot)
##
m_rs <-  lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year,
       random= ~ 1 + year |fence/wholeplot/subplot,
       data=data)

## there are only 3 blocks and 6 fences per block so unlikely to be able to estimate this fully hierarchical specification of the RE
m_hier <- lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year,
       random= ~ 1 |block/fence/wholeplot/subplot,
       data=data)

## equivalent in lme4 -- can do all of above but no corAR1
detach(package:nlme)
library(lme4)

m_simple_lmer <- lmer(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year + (1 |fence/wholeplot/subplot),
       data=data)

> > > > > > > Looking back on my notes, I think the correct DF for your experiment are Blocks= 2 (3 total-1); Fences/WW= 1 (2 per block-1); subplots/SW= 1 (2 per main plot-1).
> > > > > > >

Hi Marguerite,

One quick note: if p-values are something you are after, then the p values provided by nlme shouldn't be used. With lme4 you can use the lmerTest::anova, which provides a convenient wrapper function for better approximation of denominator degrees of freedom (Satterthwaite or Kenward-Roger) and thus more acceptable p values. See ?pvalues with lme4 loaded for more info.

best,
tim

On Thursday, December 11, 2014 2:25:27 PM UTC-5, Jaime Ashander wrote:
> Hi Marguerite,
>
> Sorry for the delay in responding. Thanks for providing the details.
>
> With the disclaimer that I Am Not a Statistician, without randomization of whole plot factors to whole plots (fence sides) and split-plot factors to subplots, the assumptions of a split-plot design aren't met. In your case the first randomization maybe isn't too meaningful (ie maybe the fence orientations are already random), but the second seems important and lacking in the design you're analyzing. Talking to a statistician seems like a good idea, but be prepared for a bad response given the lack of randomization!
>
> If the assumptions WERE met, specification of a split plot follows Pinheiro/Bates Oats example (see section 1.6 of their book, or the code available here https://www.stat.wisc.edu/courses/st850-lindstro/handouts/splitplotlme.pdf) Your example would have some differences. Below is my understanding of how they would work in nlme/lmer
>
> - In Oats each treatment of the split plot factor is only applied to one subplot, while in your case there are two, this introduces another level of nesting at the (physical) spilt plot level.  Specifying this in the Oats example would be redundant to the fixed effects on nitro (something like yield ~  Variety * ordered(nitro) + (1 | Block/Variety/nitro) which causes an error because there's one Block:Variety:nitro level for each observation!)
>
> - Your repeated measures, which are also part of the question (is there a change over time?). Specifying RE at the subplot level will also take care of this, with no need to year in the RE term. Adding year will make the model saturated. m_simple below implements this (and is the same as Emily's suggestion but without Year as the final level of RE). Simply specifying within-subplot RE doesn't formally account for temporal autocorrelation within subplot -- to do that see ?nlme::corAR1). First just look at random slope on year (see below). I think this is the best option and if the within-subplot residuals look ok corAR1 isn't necessary.
>
> - Fences within Blocks: this is worth trying to account for but there may not be the data to estimate it
>
>
> # Questions: whether carbon flux changes significantly between treatments and through time.
>
> # make unique variables for each nested unit
> # this makes sthings clearer to you and
> # if you use lme4 it will then recognize the implicit nesting
> data <- within(data, {
>     wholeplot <- factor(block:fence:WW)
>     subplot <- factor(block:fence:WW:SW)
> })
>
> m_simple <- lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year,
>        random= ~ 1 |fence/wholeplot/subplot,
>        data=data)
>
> ## this (or analogous version accounting for block) makes most sense as it allows for with subplot differences in response and could be implemented in lme or lmer
> ## it seems necessary if data show variation in temporal trend within WWWC:SCSW combinations but the fit may be unhealthy (very high correlation between slope and intercept within subplot)
> ##
> m_rs <-  lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year,
>        random= ~ 1 + year |fence/wholeplot/subplot,
>        data=data)
>
> ## there are only 3 blocks and 6 fences per block so unlikely to be able to estimate this fully hierarchical specification of the RE
> m_hier <- lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year,
>        random= ~ 1 |block/fence/wholeplot/subplot,
>        data=data)
>
> ## equivalent in lme4 -- can do all of above but no corAR1
> detach(package:nlme)
> library(lme4)
>
> m_simple_lmer <- lmer(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year + (1 |fence/wholeplot/subplot),
>        data=data)
>
>
>
> On Tue, Dec 9, 2014 at 9:47 PM, Marguerite Mauritz <mauritzm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Emily,
> >
> > I should have added that diagram to start with. Pictures are useful. I had to make that for myself when I started working on this project because I kept (and apparently still am) getting hopelessly confused.
> >
> > As far as I understand these things, I think that your suggested model is correct, but I am still not sure about including subplot in the nesting structure. It puts all my units of replication into the grouping factors and I'm not entirely sure how the model deals with that. I think that nlme doesn't like it but just ignores it, lme4 just won't run.
> >
> > Once I have triangulated various pieces of information I will post the solution I came up with. I'm also curious what Jaime will come back with.
> >
> > Thanks so much for your input, it has been really helpful!
> > Marguerite
> >
> > On Tuesday, December 9, 2014 2:54:14 PM UTC-5, Emily Peffer wrote:
> > > Oh yeah, this helps. This is different than what I was imagining. I thought each fence was entirely one WW treatment or the other, and I didn't realize there were replications of SW within the main plot.
> > >
> > > So from this diagram it looks to me like your blocks aren't really necessary to include. Normally a block is split into sub-units that are different (like plots that get different treatments) but in your case, each fence has the same combination of treatments.  Your fences are acting like blocks in this diagram, with each fence split into two main plots (WW and WC) and each main plot split into four subplots (SW and SC). If you include fence, that will take care of the spatial variation that would also be attributable to block, so I see no need to include both. So I'd structure the model like this:
> > >
> > > lme(carbon~WWWC*SCSW*Year,
> > >        random=~1|Fence/WWWC/SCSW/subplot/Year,

messages.body_plain:
Jaime,

It is true that there is no true randomisation, I have wondered about that myself. I think the rationale must have been that having replicate sub-plots was better than single, randomly placed sub-plots. That is why sub-plot is not the unit of replication for SW effects. However, I was not part of the experimental design, so I am not sure.

Am I correct in thinking the recoding of subplot, as you have written it, would not include two replicates for each SW treatment? That code would basically create a new ID in which the two SW treatments in each WW treatment are averaged.

As far as specifying covariance structure, wouldn't I have to include the correlation? Because subplot has been redefined block:fence:WW:SW the unit of repeated measure will not be each individual sub-plot but the combined sub-plots, right?
I need to look at the data with this specifically in mind and see how different the slopes through time are for each plot. I expect they are quite different and that an average does not really capture it.

m_rs <-  lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year,
       random= ~ 1 + year |fence/wholeplot/subplot,

       correlation=corAR1(form=~year|fence/wholeplot/subplot)
       data=data)

**not sure whether I have to actually repeat the random structure in corCAR1(), I can look that up.

The ultimate goal is to start doing continuous analyses and moving away from the ANOVA and categorical treatment effects. We want to consider the full range of environmental conditions which arise from the manipulation. However, I want to get the ANOVA right because I think I'll want to use it to set the stage. I want to get the random structure right because I will continue to have to either account for it or at least test it's importance.

Marguerite

On Thursday, December 11, 2014 2:25:27 PM UTC-5, Jaime Ashander wrote:
> Hi Marguerite,
>
> Sorry for the delay in responding. Thanks for providing the details.
>
> With the disclaimer that I Am Not a Statistician, without randomization of whole plot factors to whole plots (fence sides) and split-plot factors to subplots, the assumptions of a split-plot design aren't met. In your case the first randomization maybe isn't too meaningful (ie maybe the fence orientations are already random), but the second seems important and lacking in the design you're analyzing. Talking to a statistician seems like a good idea, but be prepared for a bad response given the lack of randomization!
>
> If the assumptions WERE met, specification of a split plot follows Pinheiro/Bates Oats example (see section 1.6 of their book, or the code available here https://www.stat.wisc.edu/courses/st850-lindstro/handouts/splitplotlme.pdf) Your example would have some differences. Below is my understanding of how they would work in nlme/lmer
>
> - In Oats each treatment of the split plot factor is only applied to one subplot, while in your case there are two, this introduces another level of nesting at the (physical) spilt plot level.  Specifying this in the Oats example would be redundant to the fixed effects on nitro (something like yield ~  Variety * ordered(nitro) + (1 | Block/Variety/nitro) which causes an error because there's one Block:Variety:nitro level for each observation!)
>
> - Your repeated measures, which are also part of the question (is there a change over time?). Specifying RE at the subplot level will also take care of this, with no need to year in the RE term. Adding year will make the model saturated. m_simple below implements this (and is the same as Emily's suggestion but without Year as the final level of RE). Simply specifying within-subplot RE doesn't formally account for temporal autocorrelation within subplot -- to do that see ?nlme::corAR1). First just look at random slope on year (see below). I think this is the best option and if the within-subplot residuals look ok corAR1 isn't necessary.
>
> - Fences within Blocks: this is worth trying to account for but there may not be the data to estimate it
>

>     subplot <- factor(block:fence:WW:SW)

>

messages.body_plain:
Marguerite,

Yes good catch. I didn't intend to suggest grouping by SW/SC and was careless in defining that subplot. Looking back remember you already have a plot variable. I intended to use that but define it as unique within each plot, so replacing that line with

    subplot <- factor(block:fence:plot)
will do what I intended. I also realized that what I wrote below referring to nesting in the subplot level ( "this introduces another level of nesting at the (physical) spilt plot level.") isn't strictly true _except_ for in the repeated measures context in which you're working. Just a minor point.

About the randomization, not being an expert in exp design I find it hard to speculate. In any case, it does seem to bring up issues where the SW/SC effect is confounded with spatial location within each fence:WW combination. The residuals within your groups when you fit the models below might indicate the degree to which there is a problem.

I would really just try to do the random slopes model alone before using the corAR1 stuff, and examine residuals to determine if that is even necessary

- Jaime

On Thu, Dec 11, 2014 at 2:18 PM, Marguerite Mauritz <mauritzm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Jaime,
>
>
> It is true that there is no true randomisation, I have wondered about that myself. I think the rationale must have been that having replicate sub-plots was better than single, randomly placed sub-plots. That is why sub-plot is not the unit of replication for SW effects. However, I was not part of the experimental design, so I am not sure.
>
> Am I correct in thinking the recoding of subplot, as you have written it, would not include two replicates for each SW treatment? That code would basically create a new ID in which the two SW treatments in each WW treatment are averaged.
>
> As far as specifying covariance structure, wouldn't I have to include the correlation? Because subplot has been redefined block:fence:WW:SW the unit of repeated measure will not be each individual sub-plot but the combined sub-plots, right?
> I need to look at the data with this specifically in mind and see how different the slopes through time are for each plot. I expect they are quite different and that an average does not really capture it.
>
> m_rs <-  lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year,
>        random= ~ 1 + year |fence/wholeplot/subplot,
>        correlation=corAR1(form=~year|fence/wholeplot/subplot)
>        data=data)
>
> **not sure whether I have to actually repeat the random structure in corCAR1(), I can look that up.
>
> The ultimate goal is to start doing continuous analyses and moving away from the ANOVA and categorical treatment effects. We want to consider the full range of environmental conditions which arise from the manipulation. However, I want to get the ANOVA right because I think I'll want to use it to set the stage. I want to get the random structure right because I will continue to have to either account for it or at least test it's importance.
>
> Marguerite
>
>
> On Thursday, December 11, 2014 2:25:27 PM UTC-5, Jaime Ashander wrote:
> > Hi Marguerite,
> >
> > Sorry for the delay in responding. Thanks for providing the details.
> >
> > With the disclaimer that I Am Not a Statistician, without randomization of whole plot factors to whole plots (fence sides) and split-plot factors to subplots, the assumptions of a split-plot design aren't met. In your case the first randomization maybe isn't too meaningful (ie maybe the fence orientations are already random), but the second seems important and lacking in the design you're analyzing. Talking to a statistician seems like a good idea, but be prepared for a bad response given the lack of randomization!
> >
> > If the assumptions WERE met, specification of a split plot follows Pinheiro/Bates Oats example (see section 1.6 of their book, or the code available here https://www.stat.wisc.edu/courses/st850-lindstro/handouts/splitplotlme.pdf) Your example would have some differences. Below is my understanding of how they would work in nlme/lmer
> >
> > - In Oats each treatment of the split plot factor is only applied to one subplot, while in your case there are two, this introduces another level of nesting at the (physical) spilt plot level.  Specifying this in the Oats example would be redundant to the fixed effects on nitro (something like yield ~  Variety * ordered(nitro) + (1 | Block/Variety/nitro) which causes an error because there's one Block:Variety:nitro level for each observation!)
> >
> > - Your repeated measures, which are also part of the question (is there a change over time?). Specifying RE at the subplot level will also take care of this, with no need to year in the RE term. Adding year will make the model saturated. m_simple below implements this (and is the same as Emily's suggestion but without Year as the final level of RE). Simply specifying within-subplot RE doesn't formally account for temporal autocorrelation within subplot -- to do that see ?nlme::corAR1). First just look at random slope on year (see below). I think this is the best option and if the within-subplot residuals look ok corAR1 isn't necessary.
> >
> > - Fences within Blocks: this is worth trying to account for but there may not be the data to estimate it
> >
> >
> > # Questions: whether carbon flux changes significantly between treatments and through time.
> >
> > # make unique variables for each nested unit
> > # this makes sthings clearer to you and
> > # if you use lme4 it will then recognize the implicit nesting

> >     wholeplot <- factor(block:fence:WW)
> >     subplot <- factor(block:fence:WW:SW)
> > })
> >
> > m_simple <- lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year,

> >        data=data)
> >
> > ## this (or analogous version accounting for block) makes most sense as it allows for with subplot differences in response and could be implemented in lme or lmer
> > ## it seems necessary if data show variation in temporal trend within WWWC:SCSW combinations but the fit may be unhealthy (very high correlation between slope and intercept within subplot)
> > ##
> > m_rs <-  lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year,
> >        random= ~ 1 + year |fence/wholeplot/subplot,
> >        data=data)
> >
> > ## there are only 3 blocks and 6 fences per block so unlikely to be able to estimate this fully hierarchical specification of the RE
> > m_hier <- lme(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year,
> >        random= ~ 1 |block/fence/wholeplot/subplot,
> >        data=data)
> >
> > ## equivalent in lme4 -- can do all of above but no corAR1
> > detach(package:nlme)
> > library(lme4)
> >
> > m_simple_lmer <- lmer(carbon ~ WWWC * SCSW * year + (1 |fence/wholeplot/subplot),
> >        data=data)
> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I have a task that's in essence simple to do, but that's taking way too long to finish in R.  It's the sort long loop task (in this case over 500,000 iterations) that one should not do in R, but since I was working in R already I tried doing it in R.  I initialized an empty object of the correct dimension and let it run for ~11 hours, but it still wasn't done  ...so I stopped it.

Although I'm about to shift to python to accomplish what I need, I'm now curious as to whether or not it can be done in R at reasonable speed with apply().  I couldn't figure out how to do it with apply(), so I defaulted to fro loops.

I have a genotypic matrix that has 440 genotype lines of a QTL population as its rows and 1049 "bins" as its columns.  The "bins" are genomic chunks at which the entire population is either homozygous for parent-1 = 0, heterozygous = 1, or homozygous for parent-2 = 2; essentially for a given bin a line has 0, 1, or 2 depending on its genotype at that bin.

What I'm trying to do is to take this genotypic matrix and expand its columns to include all pairwise epistatic interactions among the 1049 bins.  The epistatic columns' "genotype" is simply the multiplication of a given pair of bin genotype vectors.  I tried to do this with nested for() loops, as you can see in the attached R script.  However, it's just way too slow in R, which I kind of feared it would be.  After all, it's 549676 new columns that need to be calculated, inserted, and named.  As I said, I tried to speed it up by appending an empty matrix of the correct size to the original matrix (knowing that R takes longer if it has to resize/enlarge objects), but it's still taking way too long.

So, I'm hoping that y'all can help turn my nested loops into an apply() or nested apply()s.  I'm attaching my code and the genotype matrix.

By the way, I think the combn() function may be able to do what I need, but I don't know if I can feed it a matrix and am still getting my head around how to structure the custom function to use with combn() to achieve what I need.  I'm thinking that I can feed combn() a list of the bin/column vectors instead of a matrix.

Thanks in advance for your help!!
Dan Fulop.

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

No need to use apply(); combn() takes simplify=FALSE to it returns a list. This allows you to use mclapply() from the parallel package. With four cores on my Macbook Pro, this takes:

> system.time(tmp <- mclapply(combn(ncol(geno.mat), 2, simplify=FALSE), function(i) geno.mat[, i[1]] * geno.mat[, i[2]], mc.cores=4))
   user  system elapsed
 44.684  13.527  73.109

Then cbind() these together with:

res <- do.call(cbind, tmp)

which takes a few seconds. I haven't really checked the results, but they look like everything worked out (please double check!):

# quick check
> combn(ncol(geno.mat), 2, simplify=FALSE)[[1]]
[1] 1 2
> all(res[, 1] == geno.mat[, 1] * geno.mat[, 2])
[1] TRUE

Overall, this is the fastest approach. apply() won't be any faster because it can't be parallelized and choose(ncol(geno.mat), 2) * ncol(geno.mat) is a lot of floating point ops (and the most expensive part is likely accessing the columns unnecessarily in apply()).

Are you sure you want to multiply these 0, 1, 2 encoded genotypes for interactions? Having no alternate alleles (a 0) will zero out everything...

HTH,
Vince

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vince,

Thanks a ton!!

As to multiplying the encoded genotypes, I was wrestling with this myself until I talked to Jie Peng, a statistician who's collaborated with us on previous QTL projects.  Sure, it implies a certain genetic architecture (both loci contribute equally to the epistatic effect and both must be present in order to have an effect), but relaxing those assumptions would require fitting additional parameters for which we don't have data.  Also, the individual (non-epistatic) bins are still included, so they're possible independent effect (independent of an epistatic effect) is still accounted for.

It might be worth pointing out that the QTL population is not a RIL pop., but rather a mix of BC2 and BC3 lines back-crossed to parent-1; parent-1 is encoded as 0, and is included in the phenotypic data and mapping analysis.  Perhaps the back-crossed design makes the choice of epistatic encoding more palatable?

Could you elaborate what you have in mind as an alternative to multiplication?

Incidentally, the purpose of building the expanded genotypic matrix is to use it in a penalized/regularized regression to infer additive and epistatic QTL simultaneously without restricting the epistatic interactions to those QTL that possess additive effects.  We're using a method (sparsenet) that implements the MC+ penalty family, which is a combination of L1 (lasso) and L0 (best subset) penalties.

Cheers,
Dan.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Davis R users,

I'm using the packages 'nlme' and 'lsmeans' to run a mixed model. My model looks like this: mod <- lme(sq_yield ~ factor1*factor2 + cov1 + cov2, random= ~1|site, data=df). I replicated a factorial design (factor1*factor2) over multiple sites and across two seasons. Site is entered as a random variable. I also have two covariates as fixed effects. I want to create a bar graph with my least squares means grouped by factor2. I can get the LS means through the command lsmeans(mod, pairwise ~ factor1*factor2), but I have not found anything that allows you to create a plot of the means. I thought about taking the LS mean values and graphing them, but I want it to have the SE bars as well. Another wrinkle is that my yield was square root transformed, so I would actually like the plot to have the back-transformed squared LS means.

Does anyone have experience doing this? I would love a hand!

Best,

Lauren

Hi Lauren,

I haven't used lsmeans much, but just the other day I ran across an answer on SO from Ben Bolker that does something quite close http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/117641/how-trustworthy-are-the-confidence-intervals-for-lmer-objects-through-effects-pa

His example code gets you partway there if you use geom_pointrange or geom_errorbar instead of geom_linerange. Below is an example modifying on his code.

Hope this helps,
Jaime

PS As for the back-transform, it seems simplest to do it on the data.frame you get from lsmeans prior to adding the coefficient labels, i.e. c4 <- c4^2 in the code below

library(lme4)
fm2 <- lmer(strength ~ batch - 1 + (1 | cask), Pastes)

library(lsmeans)
c4 <- with(summary(lsmeans(fm2,spec="batch")),cbind(lsmean, lower.CL,upper.CL))

library(ggplot2); theme_set(theme_bw())

allCI <-    data.frame(
               setNames(as.data.frame(c4),
                        c("mean", "lwr","upr")))
allCI[['batch']] <- gsub('batch', '', names(fixef(fm2))) ## need to carefully modify for > 1 fixef!
ggplot(allCI, aes(batch, y=mean, ymin=lwr,ymax=upr))+
    geom_pointrange(position=position_dodge(width=0.8))

## with several interactions as you have, may be more straightforward to do
## allCI[['coef']] <- names(fixef(fm2))
##ggplot(allCI, aes(coef, y=mean, ymin=lwr,ymax=upr))+

messages.body_plain:
Greetings D-RUG Hive Mind!

We are perplexed by a seemingly simple contrast that we are running via glht on a glm.nb model to determine differences between levels of an interaction term on a negative binomial glm. The differences are significant as we would think they would be (see barplot) except that there are no significant differences between the other levels and a level that is all zero, 2012.

Certainly if there is a difference between the 2013 - Broad habitat and all others there should be similar or identical differences with 2012!

We do get a common error when we run the model because of the non-integer response, but I think the analysis is still appropriate because these are in fact count data. Our methods necessitate that we scale them slightly to conduct the comparisons between site types.

Thanks in advance for your feedback. A brief script version and dataset are attached. It would be excellent if you could reply to all to continue to include Karen (at UCSC) in the conversation.

Thanks!

Kara & Karen

--
Kara Moore
Assistant Project Scientist
Center for Population Biology
Department of Evolution and Ecology
University of California, Davis
http://dynamicecosciences.wordpress.com/

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kara and Karen,

I believe the strange behavior of glht is due to zero variance within the 2012 level of factor Season. This blows up the SE on the test being used for the contrast, resulting in non-signifcance.

A larger issue is this data doesn't seem negative binomial at all the combinations of factor levels that the model attempts to predict, leading to poor performance of the model (see some diagnostic plots below). Dropping 2012 from the analysis helps a bit, but issues remain. I would look into a zero-inflated model with at least Season as a predictor of the probability of getting a zero!

Hope this helps,
Jaime

## this data isn't negative binomial within levels of the predictors!
ggplot(all_habitat, aes(Season, Density_100)) + geom_jitter()

## resid v fitted -- model understantably struggles to get those 2012 zeroes
plot(t2, which=1)

## qqplot is ugly - should be somewhat linear
plot(t2, which=2)

library(ggplot2)

all_habitat$resid <- resid(t2)
all_habitat$fitted <- predict(t2, type='response')

## residuals by year -- systematic underprediction within the non-2012 years
ggplot(all_habitat, aes(Season, resid)) + geom_jitter()
ggplot(all_habitat, aes(fitted, resid)) + geom_jitter() + geom_smooth(method='lm') +
    geom_hline(xintercept=0) + facet_wrap(~Season)

## try without 2012
ahb2 <- all_habitat[all_habitat$Season != 2012, ]
ahb2$Season <- factor(ahb2$Season)
ahb2$HabitatSeason <- interaction(ahb2$Habitat, ahb2$Season, drop=T) # put interaction into a column in the data frame
t3<-glm.nb(Density_100 ~HabitatSeason, data=ahb2) # run another model

## qqplot -- still trouble
plot(t3, which=2)

## resid v fitted -- doesn't seem to help with underprediction
plot(t3, which=1)

ggplot(ahb2, aes(Season, resid)) + geom_jitter()
(g <- ggplot(ahb2, aes(fitted, resid)) + geom_jitter() + geom_smooth(method='gam') + geom_hline(xintercept=0))
g + facet_wrap(~Season)

ahb2$Den<-round(ahb2$Density_100*100)
m_zi <- zeroinfl(Den ~HabitatSeason | Season, data = ahb2, dist = "negbin", EM = TRUE)
m_nb <- glm.nb(Den~ HabitatSeason, data=ahb2)
vuong(m_zi, m_nb)

Shows that the zero inflated model is a bit better.

The next piece of the puzzle is to work out how to do something like a contrast between levels of within HabitatSeason. I've been exploring that a bit and see two viable options. 1) going back to glmmADMB, which I'm more familiar with, using AIC to compare models, then glht() to get a tukey's test, or 2) comparing CI around the coefficients using
(est <- cbind(Estimate = coef(m1), confint(m1)))
and/or
exp(est) to look at the CI around incidence rate ratios as suggest by the ucla page: http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/r/dae/nbreg.htm

Thanks for the discussion and the excellent pointers!

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Accessing t-1 in ode model
messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: Accessing t-1 in ode model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rachel,

If you are just looking to access the variable t, I’m not sure why you wouldn’t be able to access it in a normal f(t, y, parms, ...) derivative function. However, the normal way to access lagged variables is to use the dede() (delay differential equation) function. See ?dede for more details, but basically you access previous values with the lagvalue() and lagderiv() calls, e.g., calling lagvalue(t-1) inside your derivative function returns a vector of state variables from t-1. Note you need to use some sort of if statement to deal with t < 0. There are good examples in the help file.

Noam

messages.body_plain:
I think you will probably have to re-calculate the intermediate value you describe if you need both its current and its lagged value in order to calculate the next derivative. I don’t believe either lagvalue() or lagderiv() can provide intermediate values that you may return from your derivative function (e.g., “inter*” in return(list(c(dx, dy), c(inter1, inter2)).

Depending on your exact application, you might not have to calculate it twice, but I’d need to see the code/problem to see.
​
Noam

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I received this inquiry from a visually-impaired bioinformatics graduate student seeking R tutoring. Please get in touch with him if you are interested.

---------- Forwarded message ---------
From: thomas hahn <thomas....@gmail.com>
Date: Tue Dec 23 2014 at 6:15:37 PM
Subject: Help with finding R tutors for microarray analysis, next generation sequencing and constructing gene interaction networks needed
To: <noam...@gmail.com>

I am a visually impaired bioinformatics graduate student using microarray data for my master’s thesis aimed at deciphering the mechanism by which the yeast wild type can suppress the rise of free reactive oxygen species (ROS) induced by caloric restriction (CR) but the Atg15 and Erg6 knockout mutant cannot.

​Since my remaining vision is very limited I need very high magnification.  But that makes my visual field very small.  Therefore I need somebody to guide me remotely through the R environment and teach me how to best use the R packages for bioinformatics, especially for microarray analysis, next generation sequencing and constructing gene and pathway interaction networks.  This is very difficult for me to figure out without assistance because Zoomtext, my magnification and text to speech software, on which I am depending because I am almost blind, has problems reading out aloud many R related websites to me.  And even those websites it can read, it can only read sequentially from left to right and then from top to bottom.  Unfortunately, this way of acquiring, finding, selecting and processing new information and answering my questions is too tiresome, ineffective and especially way too time consuming for graduating with a PhD in bioinformatics before my funding runs out despite being severely limited by my visual disability.

Since I am legally blind the rehab agency is giving me money to pay tutors for this purpose.  Could you please help me getting in touch regarding this with anybody, who could potentially be interested in teaching me R thus saving me time for acquiring new information and skills, which I need to finish my thesis on time, so that I can remain eligible for funding to continue in my bioinformatics PhD program despite being almost blind?  The tutoring can be done remotely via TeamViewer 5 and Skype.  Hence, it does not matter where my tutors are physically located.  Currently I have tutors in Croatia and UK.  But since they both work full time jobs while working on their PhD dissertation they only have very limited time to teach me online.  Could you therefore please forward this request for help to anybody, who could potentially be interested or, who could connect me to somebody, who might be, because my graduation and career depend on it?  Who else would you recommend me to contact regarding this?

I thank you very much in advance for your thoughts, ideas, suggestions, recommendations, time, help, efforts and support.

With very warm regards,

Thomas Hahn

Cell phone: (318) 243 3940

Skype ID: tfh002

Preferred email: Thomas....@gmail.com
